comments.story_title: Porting 30K lines of code from Flow to TypeScript
comments.why_zh: Hickey 的 spec 思路对可选性与数据形状的处理
comments.quote_zh: 能够把一个对象的形状 spec 出来，然后在需要其中部分数据的不同上下文里，明确指定你需要什么，这是对可选性（optionality）的一个极佳解法（去看那场演讲！）。
comments.text_zh: 我在 TypeScript 和 Clojure 之间来回摇摆。我一直在密切关注 Clojure 即将推出的 spec，因为它看起来是一个很不错的选择性启用的运行时类型检查方案。我喜欢动态语言带来的灵活性和快速迭代，但我也想要安全性。我至少想兼得两者的部分好处。所以没错，它们（动态类型语言）确实有一些优势。有时我在快速迭代时，尤其是在新项目上，我不想跟编译器较劲。但是，比起 JavaScript，我远远更喜欢 TypeScript，因为 JS 有很多容易踩的坑。我觉得等我们有了 existential operator，坑会少一些，但我大概再也不会在工作中用 JS 从零开始写新项目了。我真的很喜欢 Rich Hickey 在最近那次 Clojure conj 演讲中提出的想法：[VIDEO] 能够把一个对象的形状 spec 出来，然后在需要其中部分数据的不同上下文里，明确指定你需要什么，这是对可选性（optionality）的一个极佳解法（去看那场演讲！）。我特别欣赏 RH 在 Clojure 设计上投入的思考，我认为 spec 的最终版本将会是动态性与选择性启用的安全性之间近乎完美的平衡。当然，TS 是 JS 的超集，所以一点点地采用它，差不多就能让我得到想要的那种平衡。
comments.text: I bounce back and forth between TypeScript and Clojure. I've been keeping a close eye on Clojure's upcoming spec as it seems to be a nice opt-in, run-time type-checking solution. I like the flexibility and quickness with which dynamic languages let me iterate, but I want the safety. I want at least some of the benefits of both. So yes, they (dynamically typed languages) have some advantages. Sometimes when I'm iterating quickly, especially on new projects, I don't want to fight with the compiler. BUT, I vastly prefer TypeScript to JavaScript because JS has a lot of foot-guns. I think when we get the existential operator, it will have less foot-guns, but I will probably never again write a new project for work in JS from scratch. I really love the ideas Rich Hickey put forth in his most recent Clojure conj talk: [VIDEO] The ability to spec out the shape of an object, and then in the different contexts in which you need some of that data, specify what you need, is an awesome solution to optionality (Watch the talk!). I absolutely love how much thought RH has put into the design of Clojure, and I think the final release of spec will be a close to perfect balance of dynamism and opt-in safety. Of course, TS is a superset of JS, so adopting it little by little sorta gets me that balance I want.

comments.why_zh: 说明数据形状，并讨论 Maybe 类型的问题
comments.quote_zh: 我推荐 Rich Hickey 大约一周前那场叫“Maybe Not”的演讲
comments.text_zh: 既然它和这个话题如此接近，我推荐 Rich Hickey 大约一周前那场叫“Maybe Not”的演讲。它主要讲的是如何指定一个函数需要（作为输入接收）和提供（作为输出发出）的数据形状，但其中也包含了一段关于 Option/Maybe 类型问题的非常精彩的讨论。总之，我的感觉是，我不理解人们在这里期望发生什么。由于误解、错误假设或其他错误，你期望自己拥有某样东西，而实际上你并没有。空引用异常（或等价物）只是症状。null 不是问题，问题是我们那些不断犯愚蠢错误的愚蠢大脑。Option/Maybe 确实迫使你处理这种情况：你请求某样东西时却没得到任何东西。但正如 Hickey 在演讲中指出的，它并非全是好处，是有代价的，而从来没人谈这个代价。当我给你一个 id 并要求返回一个 Book 对象时，我想要拿回一个 Book，而不是一个 `Maybe Book`。这个概念不能映射到现实世界中的任何东西，而且在实际使用中也有问题。（例如，我的函数从也许给你一个 Book、也许不给，变成一定会提供一个 Book。于是我把它的返回类型从 `Maybe Book` 改成 `Book`。只不过，哎呀，我刚刚破坏了我函数的所有调用方，尽管我加强了函数所提供数据的保证。这不应该破坏任何人才对。）[VIDEO]（关于 Option/Maybe 的讨论从
comments.text: Since it's so close to this topic, I recommend Rich Hickey's talk from about a week ago, called "Maybe Not". It's mostly about the issue of how to specify the shape of data a function requires (takes as input) and provides (emits as output), but it also contains a really nice discussion of problems with Option/Maybe types. Anyway, my feeling is that I don't understand what people expect to happen here. Due to a misunderstanding, bad assumption, or other error, you expected to have something when you actually don't have the thing. A null-reference exception (or equivalent) is just the symptom. Null isn't the problem, our dumb brains that constantly make dumb mistakes are the problem. Option/Maybe does force you to deal with the case that you didn't get anything when you asked for something. But as Hickey points out in his talk, it isn't all benefit, there is a cost, and nobody ever talks about the cost. When I provide you an id and ask for a Book object in return, I want a Book back, not a `Maybe Book`. This concept does not map to anything in the real world, and it has problems in practical usage as well. (e.g. My function changes from maybe giving you a Book or maybe not, to definitely providing you a Book. So I change its return type from `Maybe Book` to `Book`. Except, oops, I just broke every single caller of my function, even though I strengthened the guarantee of the data my function will provide. That shouldn't break anyone.) [VIDEO] (Discussion of Option/Maybe starts

comments.author: nerdponx
comments.story_title: Some thoughts about raising the profile of Lisp
comments.why_zh: 关于类型的深思熟虑看法，切中 Clojure 核心
comments.quote_zh: 对编程中的“类型”一种不寻常但深思熟虑的看法，我认为它切中了 Clojure 的核心。
comments.text_zh: 有道理，我以为那是挖苦，所以也用挖苦回应了。我觉得你应该两个都试试。Lisp 作为语言给你的自由比 Clojure 多得多，但 Clojure 的语言设计更一致、更优雅。Clojure 专注于以不可变数据结构为主的、近乎纯函数式的编程，而 Lisp 让你几乎在任何地方做任何事，包括深入运行时本身去折腾（Clojure 在一定程度上也能这么做，但不如 Lisp 那么多）。有几个值得看的视频，合在一起我觉得能很好地感受到这两种语言的区别：- Alan Diepert 的 “Common Lisp for the Curious Clojurian”。非常清晰地并排比较了 Clojure 和 Common Lisp；假定你有一些 Clojure 知识，但其实并不太需要。[LINK] - Rich Hickey 的 “Maybe Not”。对编程中的“类型”一种不寻常但深思熟虑的看法，我认为它切中了 Clojure 的核心。[VIDEO] - “Immutable Conversations - Common Lisp”，对 Alejandro Serrano 和 Michał “phoe” Herda 的采访。展示了 Common Lisp 运行时的深度可编程性和灵活性，包括其独特的“条件系统”。[LINK]
comments.text: Fair enough, I thought it was snark so I responded with snark. I think you should try both. Lisp as a language gives you a lot more freedom than Clojure, but Clojure has a more consistent and elegant language design. Clojure focuses on mostly-pure functional programming with immutable data structures, while Lisp lets you do pretty much anything anywhere, including hacking deep into the runtime itself (Clojure lets you do this to some extent too, but not as much as Lisp). Some videos that are worth viewing, which together I think provide a good sense of how the languages differ: - "Common Lisp for the Curious Clojurian" by Alan Diepert. A very lucid side-by-side comparison of Clojure and Common Lisp; assumes some but doesn't really require much knowledge of Clojure. [LINK] - "Maybe Not" by Rich Hickey. An unusual but thoughtful take on "types" in programming, which I think cuts to the heart of what Clojure is all about. [VIDEO] - "Immutable Conversations - Common Lisp" interview with Alejandro Serrano and Michał "phoe" Herda. Demonstrates the deep programmability and flexibility of the Common Lisp runtime, including its unique "condition system". [LINK]

comments.author: chubot
comments.story_title: Cap'n Proto 1.0
comments.why_zh: 很好地解释了 schema 和版本控制中 Maybe 的问题
comments.quote_zh: Rich Hickey（Clojure 语言的创造者）有一个很好的演讲 "Maybe Not"，谈到了这些问题，并且用很好的方式解释了它
comments.text_zh: Rich Hickey（Clojure 语言的创造者）有一个很好的演讲 "Maybe Not"，谈到了这些问题，并且用很好的方式解释了它 [VIDEO] capnproto 那个链接用一个 message bus 的例子具体解释了这一点，这很有用。但更抽象地说，你可以把数据的形状（也就是 schema、名称和类型）与字段存在性（optional/required）看作彼此分离的东西 [LINK] 首先，相对于静态类型系统而言是有效还是无效，是程序的 GLOBAL 属性——写一个类型检查器就会让你相信这一点。而大型分布式系统并不具备这种全局属性：[LINK] 如果它们有，那它们就会很小 :) 也就是说，你可以直接一次性重启整个东西。你没法一次性重启整个互联网，而这对更小的系统也同样成立，比如 Google 的那些系统（我相信 Cloudflare 等也是如此）。所以想法是：shape/schema 是 GLOBAL 属性——你永远不希望有两个都叫 foo.RequestX 的消息，或者两个都叫 "num_bar" 但类型不同的字段。但 optional/required 是 LOCAL 属性。它取决于某个特定二进制中部署的是哪个版本的 schema。从本质上说，你需要能够处理同时运行的不一致版本混合。--- 严格来说，我会说“making illegal states unrepresentable”确实适用，但你不能在 STATIC 类型系统里做到。你的 Maybe<T> 类型对于跨进程边界的数据没有用。分布式系统不是状态机。1. Lamport 向我们展示了
comments.text: Rich Hickey (creator of the Clojure language) has a good talk "Maybe Not" that touches on these issues, with a nice way of explaining it [VIDEO] The capnproto link explains it concretely in terms of a message bus example, which is useful. But more abstractly you can think of the shape of data (aka schema, names and types) and field presence (optional/required) as separate things [LINK] First, being valid or invalid with respect to a static type system is a GLOBAL property of program -- writing a type checker will convince you of that. And big distributed systems don't have such global properties: [LINK] If they did, they'd be small :) Namely you could just reboot the whole thing at once. You can't reboot say the entire Internet at once, and this also holds for smaller systems, like the ones at say Google (and I'm sure Cloudflare, etc.). So the idea is that the shape/schema is a GLOBAL property -- you never want two messages called foo.RequestX or two fields called "num_bar" with different types, ever. But optional/required is LOCAL property. It depends on what version of a schema is deployed in a particular binary. Inherently, you need to be able to handle a mix of inconsistent versions running simultaneously. --- To be pedantic, I woulds say "making illegal states unrepresentable" DOES apply, but you can't do it in a STATIC type system. Your Maybe<T> type is not useful for data that crosses process boundaries. A distributed system isn't a state machine. 1. Lamport showed us

comments.quote_zh: 然而，`Maybe<T> | Option<T> | ...` 并不是可选项（这里有意双关），正如 Rich Hickey 在这里所解释的
comments.text_zh: 然而，`Maybe<T> | Option<T> | ...` 并不是可选项（这里有意双关），正如 Rich Hickey 在这里所解释的：[VIDEO] 。实际上，他的论点是：1）你把 `public X Do(Y y)` 改成了 `public X Do(Option<Y> y)`。这会破坏你的 API。2）你把 `public X Do(Y y)` 改成了 `Option<X> Do(Y y)`。这会破坏你的 API。因此，不要在 API 中使用 Option<T> 或类似物。只使用语言支持的构造，比如 C#8 即将推出的 `string?` 和 `string`。
comments.text: Yet `Maybe<T> | Option<T> | ...` is not an option (pun intended), as Rich Hickey explains here: [VIDEO] . In effect, his argument is: 1) You have `public X Do(Y y)` changed into `public X Do(Option<Y> y)`. This will break your API. 2) You have `public X Do(Y y)` changed into `Option<X> Do(Y y)`. This will break your API. Thus, do not use Option<T> or equivalent in your API's. Only use a language-supported construct such as C#8's upcoming `string?` and `string`.

comments.text: Rich’s point is the type signature actually tells you little about what the function does. You need the name, docs, tribal knowledge, your own understanding of the math… etc. to actually understand what it does. Type signature alone is a very incomplete understanding. But come on, do you think I learned how to write Haskell and don’t understand what a type signature’s value is? Give me a little credit. Here is Rich’s work on the subject: [VIDEO] I’m biased, but I think he’s got a point.

comments.author: zbobet2012
comments.story_title: (Next Rich)
comments.quote_zh: Maybe Not 在某些方面是一个很出色的视频
comments.text_zh: Maybe Not 在某些方面是一个很出色的视频，但我几年后再看它时，它提醒我：尽管我几乎喜欢每一个 Rich 的视频，我还是真希望他能花点时间更深一点地阅读类型系统和理论。例如，他关于 "Categorical descriptions" 的笔记，以及 25:00 处关于 maps 和 spec 的解释[1]，似乎表明他不熟悉 extensional 与 intensional type theory 之间的区别。二者的核心区别在于：extensional 类型系统根据输出的可观察行为来判定相等性。例如，如果两个函数接受相同输入并产生相同输出，extensional 类型系统/理论就说它们是相同的。问题在于，类型相等性于是就变得不可判定。Extensional 类型系统还会遇到困难，因为事物可能以不止一种方式相等！例如，两个字符串在你忽略大小写时可能相等，但不忽略时就不相等。所以，如果我们想让类型系统检查两个函数在大小写不敏感的情况下是否相等，extensional 类型系统就会很难处理这一点。[2][3] 不过为 Rich 说句公道话，这些概念更多来自数学界，尤其是类型在不同路径下相等的观念，而在 Homotopy type theory 的情况下，它们被埋在难以接近的语言和概念中……即使按数学家的标准也是如此。他还谈到从 spec 中 select，以及它不能阻止你传入更宽泛的类型，还有指定 dee 的必要性
comments.text: Maybe Not is an excellent video in some ways, but I just watched it a few years later and it reminded me that as much as I love almost every Rich video, I do wish he'd spend some time reading a little deeper on type systems and theory. For example his note about "Categorical descriptions" and then the explanation about maps/and spec at 25:00[1] seems to indicate he's unfamiliar with the difference between extensional and intensional type theory. The core difference between the two is extensional type systems decide equality on the observable behavior of the output. For example if two functions take the same input, and produce the same output extensional type systems/theories say they are the same. The problem with this is type equality is then undecidable. Extensional type systems also struggle because there are more than one way things might be equal! For example two string might be equal if you ignore case, but unequal if you don't. So if we want our type system to check if two functions are equal under case insensitivity an extensional type system will struggle with this.[2][3] Now in fairness to Rich, these concepts come more from the math community, especially the notion of types being equal under different paths, and in the case of Homotopy type theory are burred in unapproachable language and concepts... even by mathematicians standards. He also talks about select from spec, and it not preventing you from passing types broader types, and the necessity of specifying dee
